W is exactly the inverse image of the isomorphisms under γ; containing isomorphisms, two-of-three and arrow-retract closure alone are insufficient.
proof: γ(f) has right inverse γ(g)(γ(f)γ(g))^-1 and left inverse (γ(g)γ(f))^-1γ(g); a left and a right inverse coincide. Thus γ(f) and γ(g) are invertible.

statement: Let M be locally small with all small colimits, and I a set of arrows whose domains are small relative to I-cell complexes. Let Φ contain all isomorphisms and all I-cell maps (for example, contain I and be closed under pushouts, coproduct attachments and continuous transfinite compositions, including zero-length composites). Then every f factors functorially as p i with i∈Φ,p∈RLP(I), after choosing a fixed sufficiently large ordinal and colimit functors.
hypotheses: I is a set and every attaching-square collection is a set.
All colimits actually used exist.
One common smallness bound is available for the set of domains; target accessibility is optional extra strength.
The closure convention includes identities or zero-length composites.
Chosen colimit functors and a common ordinal are used for ordinary functoriality.
proof: The all-squares construction in proofs.md makes the left leg cellular; domain smallness sends every generator lifting square to a stage where the corresponding cell is attached. Functorial transport of squares extends through the chosen colimits.

statement: In a stable derivator, a coherent square is cartesian if and only if it is cocartesian; the same holds in every shift. Consequently the appropriate coherent Kan-extension squares have both properties.
hypotheses: The coefficient derivator is pointed and stable.

For the provisional Der6/dual applications, retain the (op)fibration and pointwise Kan hypotheses establishing the first exactness property.
proof: The stable square property and stability of shifts give the added exactness. The spaces counterexamples show why the stable hypothesis cannot simply be omitted.

statement: For nonempty CW spaces A,B, the homotopy-cartesian product square A×B→B, A→* is also homotopy cocartesian exactly when the unreduced join A*B is weakly contractible. This need not make either A or B contractible.
hypotheses: Use the derived pushout of the two projections from A×B and the derived product over a point.
Nonempty CW spaces ensure the ordinary join/double-mapping-cylinder model has the stated homotopy type.
proof: That homotopy pushout is the unreduced join. The acyclic noncontractible presentation complex K of P6 has K*K contractible, furnishing the checked negative witness.

statement: In an ordinary homotopy-pushout square, weak equivalence of one input leg implies weak equivalence of the opposite output leg. Reverse cancellation requires an extra hypothesis, for example detection by a coherent bicartesian coefficient square.
hypotheses: The square is a coherent homotopy pushout for the forward implication.
For the reverse coefficient implication, the chosen invariant detects the relevant W-maps and sends this square to a coherent bicartesian square.
proof: Homotopy cobase change proves the forward implication. The cartesian and cocartesian edge-isomorphism tests give the two directions under the additional coefficient hypothesis. The double cone shows the reverse is not universal for W∞.

statement: For a coherent map of bicartesian squares in a stable coefficient theory, any two of (a) terminal map invertible, (b) initial map invertible, and (c) both side maps invertible imply the third. A category-level W8 assertion follows only when W is detected by that coefficient theory and the displayed construction supplies those coherent bicartesian squares.
hypotheses: A coherent map of squares in a stable derivator or equivalent stable homotopy theory.
To transfer to categories, specify a coefficient invariant detecting W and verify that both constructed squares are bicartesian.
Smoothness/properness alone is not substituted for these stable coefficient hypotheses.
proof: The first two implications use the cartesian/cocartesian universal properties. For the remaining implication, the Mayer–Vietoris triangle makes the block-diagonal side map invertible; each summand map is then invertible.
